children.text: Built in 1972 by Cebu's Chinese-Filipino community on a Beverly Hills hilltop, this is a Chinese-style Taoist temple. You can walk its three levels of red pillars, green tiles and dragon sculptures, take in the city views and see a living tradition of worship, all for free, which makes it the easiest cultural stop to squeeze into a spare half day in Cebu City.
Cebu Taoist Temple stands on a hillside in Beverly Hills Subdivision, a gated upscale neighborhood above Lahug district, north of downtown Cebu City. It is a place of Taoist worship. In

Cebu's Chinese-Filipino community built it as the center of its faith, in honor of Laozi, the founder of Taoism. Chinese Filipinos have long been one of the pillars of commerce and culture in the Philippines, and this temple is a symbol through which that community keeps its identity.

The grounds are laid out over three levels along the slope. On each level you find halls with red pillars and green and blue tiled roofs, cloud-pattern decoration and dragon sculptures, one after another. From the lower level to the upper level run 81 steps, said to symbolize the 81 chapters of the Taoist scripture, and the way up winds along three separate routes. The entrance is said to have been built in the shape of the Great Wall of China. The plaque on the red main gate gives the temple's formal name, the Philippine Taoist Temple. Inside are a worship hall, a library, an incense and souvenir shop, a pond with a statue of an old man fishing, and gardens, and from the wide balcony you can look down on Cebu City. A sign by the pond says not to throw coins, so it is easy to mistake for a wishing well, but that is not its purpose.

What makes this place special is that it is not an exhibition hall built for tourists but a working temple where worshippers still burn incense and ask for answers through divination. Unlike the nearby Phu Sian Temple, which is not open to the general public, this one welcomes travelers who are not worshippers too, free of charge, making it one of the few places where you can see the religious life of Cebu's Chinese community up close.

It is close to downtown, there is no admission fee, and an hour or two is enough, so it slots easily into an itinerary. It suits travelers who love architecture and photography, those who want to see the layered culture of the Philippines, and families who want to combine it with Busay-area sights such as Temple of Leah and Sirao Garden for a half day.

Climbing the steps that symbolize the 81 chapters of the scripture, one level at a time, is the basic way to see the temple, and you get a feel for how it is laid out as you go. If you turn around on each landing, the rooflines, the gardens and the city in the distance come into view from slightly different angles.

The fortress-like entrance leading into the grounds sets the first impression of the temple. The red gate, the stone wall and the Chinese-character plaque fit in a single frame, so take a photo before you go in.

A dragon coils on the end of each green tiled roof, and the dragon stands for success, prosperity and protection. From the halls on the upper level you are at eye level with the roofs and can see the fine carving of scales and whiskers up close.

In the pavilion with a round window, through which bamboo shows, stands a statue of Guanyin, known as the goddess of mercy, and each level holds different statues. Slow down in front of the halls with round windows and the incense burners, and if people are praying, keep your distance and watch.

Worshippers wash their hands, take off their shoes and then throw a pair of crescent-shaped wooden blocks to ask whether their wish will be granted. The ritual is not a performance, so watch from close by only after asking the staff for permission, and do not touch any religious objects.

Gardens, a pond and small pavilions such as the Qingfeng Pavilion fill the spaces between the halls, making it a good place to catch your breath even at midday. The pond with the fisherman statue is not for throwing coins, so just look, and capture the contrast between the red pillars and green leaves in a photo.

blocks.title: City views from the upper balcony

children.text: From the wide balcony on the top level, the houses of Lahug and the buildings of downtown Cebu spread out in one view, and on a clear day you can see all the way toward Mactan. A popular shot uses the tiled eaves as a frame for the city.

blocks.title: The atmosphere at Lunar New Year

children.text: Around Lunar New Year, worshippers keep coming to offer incense and pray for blessings in the new year, and the temple takes on a deeper feeling than usual. Walking quietly through red decorations and incense smoke is an experience you only get at this time.

items.title: A 2-hour route centered on the temple
items.subtitle: Best on a weekday morning

children.text: Leave your downtown hotel by Grab and tell the guard at the Beverly Hills gate you are visiting the temple
Take photos in front of the entrance wall, then check your shoes and clothing at the foot of the steps
Climb the steps slowly, looking over the lower halls, the gardens and the dragon sculptures
Quietly watch worshippers' divination in front of the worship hall and offer incense yourself
Rest on the upper balcony with the view of the city, then walk down along the gardens and the pond
Catch a ride back at the entrance and head to the Lahug restaurant area for lunch

A morning visit is the most comfortable. At midday the steps and stone floors heat up, and in the late afternoon you have less time because closing time is near. Opening hours differ from source to source, so check before you set out.

items.title: A half day combined with the Busay hills
items.subtitle: Based on a chartered car

looking around the grounds

Combining the three places in one car means you do not have to hail a taxi each time you go up and down. Negotiate a price that includes waiting time in advance, and wear shoes that are easy to take off and put on, since there are areas of the temple you enter without shoes.
You fly into Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB), about
1 hour 20 minutes
by direct flight from Manila. There are also direct flights from major cities in Korea, Japan and China. From the airport to the Lahug district where the temple stands, allow about
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic.
This is the simplest way. From the center of downtown Cebu it takes about
20–30 minutes
, and the fare is generally about

. The road below the temple is steep and you pass a security check at the Beverly Hills gate, so say that you are going to the Taoist temple and you will be directed. It can be hard to find a ride back at the temple, so book one in the app ahead of time or ask your driver to wait.
To save money, take a jeepney on a Lahug or Sudlon route such as 04L or 17B, get off near Sudlon, and then go up by habal-habal (motorcycle taxi). The jeepney fare is about
, and the habal-habal is negotiated at about

. Jeepneys cannot enter Beverly Hills, so the last stretch has to be done on foot uphill or by motorcycle. Route numbers can change, so ask the driver whether the jeepney goes toward Lahug when you board.

If you follow the signs toward Lahug to the entrance of the Beverly Hills subdivision, there is free parking near the temple, but spaces are limited and it can get crowded at Lunar New Year or on weekend mornings.

Many Cebu City tours and Busay hills tours include the Taoist temple. A guide adds explanations and you do not have to worry about getting around, which is convenient for first-time visitors. Some packages have short stops, so check how long you will stay in advance.
Cebu's dry season generally runs
December–May
, with clear skies that make the steps easier to climb.
January–February
is relatively cool, so you tire less walking at midday, while in
March–May
daytime temperatures rise as high as
, the hottest stretch, but the visibility makes the city views the sharpest.
In the
June–November

rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent and the steps and stone floors become slippery. On days when a typhoon or heavy rain warning is issued, the hill road is dangerous, so postpone your visit. If you aim for a rain-free morning, you can still see the temple well in the rainy season.
At Lunar New Year (Spring Festival) the temple is busier than usual and the atmosphere deepens. Lunar New Year fell on
February 17, 2026

and the date changes every year, so check it separately if you want to go then. It is said that every Wednesday and Sunday worshippers climb the steps to burn incense and receive a fortune reading, so if you want to see the ritual atmosphere, those days are worth aiming for.

There is almost no lodging around the temple, a quiet residential neighborhood, and most visitors come from downtown Cebu. The Lahug and IT Park area is easy to find restaurants and shops on foot and is
20–30 minutes
from the temple by car, making it a convenient base, with business hotels at about
per night. For shopping and dining in one place, the area near Ayala Center Cebu is also a good choice.

There are no restaurants inside the temple, only a few simple snacks sold near the entrance, so bring drinking water with you. Cebu has deep Chinese roots, so Chinese-Filipino foods such as siopao (steamed buns), siomai and pancit are easy to find anywhere. After the temple, finish with lunch in the Lahug area, perhaps Cebu's famous lechon (roast whole pig) or charcoal-grilled skewers.
Opening hours differ from source to source. They are listed as 6 AM to 6 PM, 8 AM to 5 PM and 9 AM to 5 PM, so if you plan to go in the late afternoon, call the temple at +63 32 254 6503 to check.
On a weekday early in the morning there are few tourists, so it is quietest, while late in the afternoon it may close early and you will feel rushed.

When you enter the worship hall, follow the order of taking off your shoes and washing your hands. Avoid sleeveless tops, short skirts and ripped clothing, and if possible wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees.
There are many steps and stone paths, so sturdy-soled sneakers are best, and since there is no restaurant inside the temple, bring water and a hat.
Some places say that photography is prohibited inside the prayer rooms. Ask the staff for permission before taking pictures.
If you want to offer incense or candles, use ones bought at the shop by the entrance, and keep small bills handy for change.
It can be hard to find a ride back, so book a Grab in advance or ask your driver to wait.
The temple is also a photo spot, but keep your voice low so as not to disturb worshippers at prayer, and do not walk in front of people who are praying.
The temple is a place where worshippers actually pray. Opening hours, photography rules and access arrangements can change without notice, so check the latest announcements before you visit.
The temple is inside a residential neighborhood, so you go through a security check at the entrance. Avoid making a fuss and drive slowly on the roads in the subdivision.
After rain the stone steps and floors are slippery. Wear shoes with good grip rather than slippers.
Do not touch or lean on the statues, incense burners or objects on the altars. It is polite not to touch religious objects without permission.
When you ride a habal-habal, agree on the fare in advance and ask for a helmet. The road is steep.
On days with a typhoon or heavy rain warning the hill road is dangerous, so postpone your visit.
